p1.tell: The Rockland decrease is 67 cents, not $67. One swapped detail turns pocket change into a windfall.
p1.explanation: The real New Jersey Monitor article said Rockland customers would see a 67-cent decrease. The Con swapped 'cents' for '$', turning a trivial change into a headline-grabbing $67. Every other word matches the source, which is why it looks familiar.
p1.con_line_fooled: One little number. Nobody ever checks the little number.
p1.con_line_caught: You compared it word for word. Who does that?

diff.shown: The average Rockland customer using about 650 kilowatt-hours within a billing cycle can expect their bill to decrease by $67, board staff said, and ratepayers with Atlantic City Electric will pay 5 cents less each month.
diff.original: The average Rockland customer using about 650 kilowatt-hours within a billing cycle can expect their bill to decrease by 67 cents, board staff said, and ratepayers with Atlantic City Electric will pay 5 cents less each month.

p2.tell: The 24% jump cherry-picks June 2024→June 2025; the latest year-over-year (Aug 2025→Aug 2026) is essentially flat at -0.4%.
p2.explanation: EIA data shows NJ residential prices did rise 23.9% from June 2024 (19.9¢) to June 2025 (24.65¢), but that window captures the post-capacity-auction spike. By August 2026 prices had fallen back to 24.61¢, making the most recent year-over-year change -0.4%. The post presents a stale peak as the current trend.
p2.con_line_fooled: Every number I used was true. I just left one out.
p2.con_line_caught: You went looking for the other half of the story. Rude.

diff.shown: NJ residential electricity prices surged 24% in one year — from 19.9¢ to 24.65¢ per kWh.
diff.missing: The most recent year: Aug 2025 to Aug 2026 prices changed -0.4%.
